questiontext.text: A line of thunderstorms is forecast to develop along the eastern boundary of the FIR over the next three hours. Cells are expected to be embedded within a stratiform cloud deck. Ben Gurion lies near the western boundary of the FIR and is not expected to be directly affected. Which office issues which products?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: The phenomenon is en-route within the FIR — that is the MWO's responsibility, and the EMBD qualifier on TS meets the SIGMET threshold. Because LLBG is not affected at the aerodrome, no AD WRNG is required. AFOs do not issue SIGMETs; MWOs do not issue AD WRNGs. Both products at once is the right answer only when the phenomenon affects both the FIR and the aerodrome — not the case here.

answer.text: The MWO issues a SIGMET; no AD WRNG is required because the aerodrome is not affected.
The AFO issues a SIGMET because Ben Gurion is the reference aerodrome.
Both the MWO and the AFO must issue an AD WRNG, since the FIR and the aerodrome share the same area of responsibility.
No product is required — embedded thunderstorms over an empty part of the FIR are not a SIGMET phenomenon.

questiontext.text: A nowcast and the latest radar show two isolated thunderstorm cells over the central highlands, well separated and clearly visible from the satellite. Both cells are vertically developed and producing lightning, but neither is embedded in cloud, obscured by haze, frequent, or part of a line. Which warning, if any, is appropriate?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: Thunderstorms require a qualifier — OBSC, EMBD, FRQ, or SQL — to trigger a SIGMET. Isolated cells that pilots can see and route around do not meet that threshold. ISOL/OCNL TS is explicitly an AIRMET phenomenon, not a SIGMET phenomenon. Issuing a SIGMET here would over-issue and dilute the credibility of future SIGMETs.

answer.text: An AIRMET, because the cells are ISOL TS — below the SIGMET qualifier threshold.
A SIGMET, because any thunderstorm with lightning meets the SIGMET threshold.
Nothing — isolated cells do not warrant any warning product.
A WV SIGMET, because the cells are convective and vertically developed.

questiontext.text: A pilot report and the model's icing-potential field both agree that moderate clear icing is occurring in stratus between 4,000 and 7,000 ft over the northern FIR. Freezing rain is not present. What warning is appropriate?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: The SIGMET icing threshold is SEV (with or without FZRA). Moderate icing is explicitly an AIRMET phenomenon (MOD ICE), regardless of the synoptic situation. The fact that freezing rain is absent makes no difference here — FZRA is an aggravating qualifier on a SEV icing case, not a stand-alone trigger. A WV SIGMET is for volcanic ash only.

answer.text: An AIRMET for MOD ICE — moderate icing is below the SIGMET severity threshold.
A SIGMET for SEV ICE, because clear icing on its own is always severe.
A SIGMET, because icing in stratus over an FIR is by definition en-route and therefore SIGMET-worthy.
A WV SIGMET, because freezing rain is absent.

name.text: L1-Q04 — Identifying SIGMET subtype from the header

questiontext.text: An incoming bulletin begins with the WMO header WVXY31 LLBD 121400. Without reading any further, what subtype of message can you expect?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: The T1T2 data-type designator is the first two letters: WV means a SIGMET for volcanic ash. The remaining letters are the country/territory designator (XY), the bulletin number (31), and the location indicator and date/time. WS would be a standard SIGMET, WA an AIRMET, and WC a tropical-cyclone SIGMET.

answer.text: A SIGMET for volcanic ash (WV).
A standard SIGMET (WS).
An AIRMET (WA).
A SIGMET for tropical cyclone (WC).

questiontext.text: Forecast output suggests mountain-wave activity east of the central ridge. The model's vertical-velocity field shows downdrafts peaking near 2.2 m/s, and no accompanying severe-turbulence signature is forecast. Which warning is appropriate?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: A mountain wave is considered SEV only when accompanied by a downdraft of 3.0 m/s or more, or severe turbulence. Downdrafts of 1.75–3.0 m/s (or accompanying moderate turbulence) fall into MOD MTW, which is an AIRMET phenomenon. A 2.2 m/s downdraft is comfortably inside the MOD band, so AIRMET is correct — no SIGMET. "No warning at all" misses the operational risk to general aviation below FL100.

answer.text: An AIRMET for MOD MTW — 2.2 m/s is below the 3.0 m/s SEV threshold.
A SIGMET for SEV MTW — any forecast mountain wave with a measurable downdraft warrants SEV.
No warning is required because the downdraft is below 3.0 m/s.
A SIGMET, because forecast mountain waves over the central ridge are always SIGMET-worthy in the IMS.

questiontext.text: A VAAC advisory reports a thin volcanic ash layer drifting through the FIR at FL250. The ash concentration is described as "low" with patchy coverage. Is a SIGMET required?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: Volcanic ash has no severity threshold under Annex 3 — any detection within the FIR triggers a WV SIGMET. The reasoning is operational: even thin or "low concentration" ash can damage turbine engines and aircraft control surfaces, so the MWO does not get to decide whether the ash is "bad enough". Concentration and altitude bands belong in the message body, not at the issuance gate.

answer.text: Yes — a WV SIGMET is required for any detection of volcanic ash in the FIR, regardless of concentration.
No — low-concentration ash is below the SIGMET threshold.
Yes, but only as an AIRMET — thin ash at FL250 is "low-level" in the AIRMET sense.
No — ash advisories are the VAAC's responsibility; the MWO does not issue ash SIGMETs.

name.text: L2-Q01 — Decoding T1T2 in an arriving bulletin

questiontext.text: An AFTN bulletin arrives with the WMO heading WAXY12 LLBD 080900. Which two facts about this message can you state with certainty before parsing any further?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: The first two letters of the WMO header are the data-type designator T1T2. WA identifies the message as an AIRMET. The CCCC field (positions 8–11) is the disseminating communication centre — here LLBD — not the FIR. The FIR identifier appears on the first line of the message body, not in the WMO header. The sequential number 12 in ii is a bulletin number, not the SIGMET/AIRMET sequence number.

answer.text: It is an AIRMET (WA), and the disseminating communication centre is LLBD.
It is a standard SIGMET (WS), and the FIR identifier is LLBD.
It is a SIGMET for volcanic ash (WV), bulletin number 12.
It is a tropical cyclone advisory (WC), valid on day 8 at 09:00 UTC.

questiontext.text: It is 09:00 UTC on day 14. The model strongly suggests that severe icing will affect a layer over the central FIR from approximately 10:00 UTC through 19:00 UTC the same day. Which is the correct issuance strategy?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: Two timing constraints apply. First, the maximum validity of a WS SIGMET is 4 hours. A single SIGMET cannot span 10:00–19:00 (that is 9 hours). Second, issuance must not precede the expected start of the phenomenon by more than 4 hours; 09:00 UTC is within 4 hours of the 10:00 expected start, so the first SIGMET can be issued now. The right operational approach is to issue the first SIGMET with a 4-hour window starting at 10:00, then re-issue with the next sequential number when that window ends and the phenomenon is still active — not "wait until later" and not "extend the validity".

answer.text: Issue SIGMET 1 valid 141000/141400 now; re-issue with the next sequential number as each 4-hour window expires while the phenomenon persists.
Issue a single SIGMET valid 141000/141900 now — one message covering the whole expected episode.
Wait until 06:00 UTC the next day before issuing — the lead-time rule forbids issuing this far ahead.
Issue two SIGMETs at the same time: one for 1000–1400 and one for 1400–1800, each with its own sequential number.

questiontext.text: Which of the following polygons is correctly formatted according to Annex 3 for use in a SIGMET meteorological part?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: Annex 3 requires lat/lon in whole degrees or degrees-and-minutes (no decimal degrees), each point starting with the hemisphere letter (N/S/E/W), and vertices separated by space-hyphen-space. The correct option uses N3623 W04515-style points (degrees+minutes, no separator) with the prescribed separator. Decimal degrees (N36.4) are not accepted. Commas as separators are not accepted. Missing the hemisphere letter at the start of a coordinate is also not accepted — the parser keys off the leading N/S or E/W.

questiontext.text: SIGMET number 4 was issued at 06:00 UTC on day 22 with validity 220600/221000 for EMBD TS over the LLBG FIR. By 08:15 UTC the convection has dissipated and is no longer forecast to redevelop within the original validity window. Which is the correct cancellation message body (after the WMO header)?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: A SIGMET cancellation is itself a SIGMET, with the next sequential number (5), a new validity period running from the issuance time to the end of the original window (220815/221000), and a second line that references the cancelled SIGMET by both its sequential number AND its original validity (CNL SIGMET 4 220600/221000). Re-using the original validity (220600/221000) on the cancellation's first line would imply the cancellation is retroactive to 06:00. Using the same sequential number (4) would not be a valid new bulletin. Omitting the original validity from the CNL line leaves the back-reference ambiguous.

answer.text: LLBG SIGMET 5 VALID 220815/221000 LLBD- LLBG TEL-AVIV FIR CNL SIGMET 4 220600/221000=
LLBG SIGMET 4 VALID 220600/221000 LLBD- LLBG TEL-AVIV FIR CNL SIGMET 4=
LLBG SIGMET 5 VALID 220600/221000 LLBD- LLBG TEL-AVIV FIR CNL SIGMET 4=
LLBG SIGMET 5 VALID 220815/221000 LLBD- LLBG TEL-AVIV FIR CNL ALL SIGMETS=

questiontext.text: The afternoon analysis shows two distinct SIGMET-worthy phenomena over the same FIR: severe icing in stratiform cloud at 4,000–8,000 ft, and embedded thunderstorms expected to develop over the eastern boundary. Both are within the next 4 hours. What is the correct issuance pattern?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: Annex 3 prescribes one phenomenon per SIGMET. Two SIGMET-worthy phenomena means two SIGMETs — each with its own sequential number, its own polygon, and its own forecast movement. Combining them into a single message creates an ambiguous weather object that downstream parsers cannot interpret. Choosing only the "more severe" of the two leaves the other un-warned. Issuing a single SIGMET for "general adverse weather" is not a defined product.

answer.text: Two SIGMETs — one for SEV ICE and one for EMBD TS, each with its own sequential number.
One SIGMET listing both SEV ICE and EMBD TS in the meteorological part.
One SIGMET for the more severe phenomenon; the other is captured in the routine forecast.
A single combined SIGMET with the literal phenomenon code MULT and a free-text description of both.

questiontext.text: SIGMET 7 for severe turbulence over the LLBG FIR is valid 1200/1600. At 15:45 UTC the turbulence is still being reported and is forecast to persist for another 2–3 hours. What action should the MWO take just before the SIGMET expires?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: Cancellation is reserved for the case where the phenomenon has ended (or is no longer expected) within the original validity. If the phenomenon outlasts the SIGMET's validity, the correct action is to issue a new SIGMET — same phenomenon, next sequential number (8), new 4-hour validity window starting at 1600. Issuing a CNL while the phenomenon is still active would mislead consumers into thinking the hazard has passed. Extending the original SIGMET past its validity violates the 4-hour ceiling. Doing nothing leaves the hazard un-warned after 1600.

answer.text: Issue a new SIGMET 8 with a fresh 4-hour validity (e.g., 1600/2000); do not cancel SIGMET 7.
Issue a CNL SIGMET 7 message so consumers know the existing SIGMET is "rolling over".
Amend SIGMET 7's validity in place to 1200/1900.
Take no action — the validity will expire at 1600 and the hazard is then communicated through pilot reports.

questiontext.text: Radar shows a developing line of thunderstorm cells over the northern sub-area of the FIR. Visual inspection and reflectivity coverage suggest the cells occupy roughly 60% of the sub-area, with discernible gaps between adjacent cells. Intensity is moderate. What message should the MWO issue?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: Coverage between 50% and 75% with discernible separation between cells is OCNL TS — an AIRMET phenomenon. FRQ requires coverage greater than 75% with little or no separation. The cells do not need to be embedded, obscured, or in a squall line to fall under AIRMET, so a SIGMET is not warranted. "No message" misses the operational hazard to low-level traffic crossing the area.

answer.text: An AIRMET for OCNL TS over the affected sub-area.
A SIGMET for FRQ TS — once coverage exceeds 50%, FRQ applies.
A SIGMET for EMBD TS, on the basis of the line structure.
No message — moderate-intensity cells with gaps do not trigger any product.

questiontext.text: Which of the following phenomena triggers an AIRMET but has no SIGMET equivalent at any intensity?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: Cloud ceilings below 1000 ft, sustained surface winds ≥ 30 kt, visibility below 5 km, and extensive mountain obscuration are AIRMET-only phenomena — they describe the low-level environment and have no SIGMET counterpart. Severe icing and embedded thunderstorms are SIGMET phenomena (with AIRMET counterparts at lower intensity, MOD ICE and ISOL/OCNL TS). Volcanic ash is exclusively a SIGMET (WV) phenomenon.

answer.text: Cloud ceilings below 1000 ft over an extensive area.
Severe icing with freezing rain.
Embedded thunderstorms over the FIR.
Volcanic ash drifting through the FIR.

questiontext.text: The model's icing-potential field is moderate-to-strong over a stratus layer between 5,000 and 8,500 ft. A pilot report at 7,000 ft describes the icing as "moderate" with no reference to freezing rain. The synoptic situation supports persistent moderate icing for the next three hours. Which message should the MWO issue?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: Both model output and the PIREP describe the icing as moderate, and the cloud is stratiform (not convective), so MOD ICE is the correct AIRMET phenomenon. SEV ICE would require a severe PIREP or unambiguous model indication of severe icing — not present here. The presence or absence of FZRA is a qualifier on a severe case, not a standalone trigger. Doing nothing leaves a known low-level hazard un-warned.

answer.text: An AIRMET for MOD ICE.
A SIGMET for SEV ICE, because stratus icing should always be promoted to severe in winter.
A SIGMET for SEV ICE FZRA, because freezing rain is a winter default assumption.
No message — pilot reports of moderate icing are not actionable on their own.

questiontext.text: A strong synoptic pressure gradient is forecast to drive sustained 10-minute mean surface winds of 32 kt across a broad sub-area of the FIR for the next 4 hours. Gusts will be higher. Which product covers the en-route hazard to general aviation across the affected area?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: Sustained surface winds ≥ 30 kt over an extensive area is an AIRMET phenomenon (SFC WSPD ≥30KT) and has no SIGMET equivalent. The aerodrome warning is a separate product, scoped to the airport itself, and is covered in Lesson 4 — an AD WRNG does not warn the en-route GA pilot crossing the FIR. A WS WRNG addresses runway-specific wind shear, not large-scale surface winds.

answer.text: An AIRMET for SFC WSPD ≥30KT over the affected sub-area.
A SIGMET for severe surface winds, since 32 kt is well above 30 kt.
An AD WRNG, because surface winds primarily affect aerodromes.
A WS WRNG, because the winds are likely to cause runway-shear conditions.

name.text: L3-Q05 — AIRMET vs SIGMET in a borderline case

questiontext.text: A mountain-wave forecast shows downdrafts peaking at exactly 3.0 m/s along the lee slopes, with accompanying severe turbulence forecast in patches. Which warning is appropriate?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: The SEV MTW threshold is downdraft ≥ 3.0 m/s or accompanying severe turbulence. Both conditions are present here, so SIGMET is the correct call — the boundary is inclusive, not exclusive. Issuing an AIRMET for MOD MTW would under-warn the hazard. Issuing both an AIRMET and a SIGMET for the same phenomenon over the same area violates the one-phenomenon-one-message principle.

answer.text: A SIGMET for SEV MTW — the 3.0 m/s threshold is inclusive and the accompanying SEV turbulence also qualifies on its own.
An AIRMET for MOD MTW — 3.0 m/s is the upper bound of the MOD band.
Both an AIRMET (for the wave) and a SIGMET (for the turbulence) over the same area.
No warning — the model is at the boundary, so the case should be left to the routine SIGWX chart.

questiontext.text: An MWO trainee asks why the IMS issues an AIRMET for visibility <5 km in haze even though the TAFs for the affected aerodromes already mention reduced visibility. What is the correct explanation?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: The "not already in the forecast" exemption refers specifically to a low-level area forecast covering the same FIR or sub-area at AIRMET intensity — typically a GAMET. TAFs are aerodrome forecasts, not low-level area forecasts; they do not exempt the MWO from issuing an AIRMET for an en-route visibility hazard. Israel does not produce a GAMET, so the exemption almost never applies and the AIRMET is issued whenever the phenomenon and intensity criteria are met. The exemption is not a "discretionary" or "tradition" clause — it is a specific carve-out tied to the existence of a covering area forecast.

answer.text: The exemption applies only when a low-level area forecast (e.g., GAMET) covers the FIR at AIRMET intensity; TAFs are aerodrome forecasts and do not satisfy the exemption.
The exemption is purely discretionary — the MWO can choose to issue the AIRMET or rely on the TAFs.
The exemption never applies to visibility, only to ceiling and surface wind AIRMETs.
The exemption is an IMS-only tradition; in other countries the TAFs would be sufficient.

name.text: L4-Q01 — Thunderstorm AD WRNG distance threshold

questiontext.text: A severe thunderstorm cell is observed on radar 22 km south-east of the LLBG runway pattern centre, moving slowly west. The cell is producing 4 cm hail. The cell is expected to come no closer than 18 km to the runway centre over the next 2 hours. Which AD WRNG action is correct?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: The IMS AD WRNG threshold for TS/CB is "CB within 16 km of the runway-pattern centre". A cell that is forecast to come no closer than 18 km does not meet that threshold, so no AD WRNG for TS is required — even though the cell is severe and producing hail. The hail-size threshold (≥ 2 cm) is a property of CB cells at the aerodrome; it does not by itself extend the 16 km TS distance criterion. Issuing an AD WRNG anyway would over-warn and waste credibility; the en-route hazard is captured separately by SIGMET/AIRMET.

answer.text: No AD WRNG for TS — the cell stays outside the 16 km IMS threshold. Consider SIGMET/AIRMET for the en-route hazard.
Issue an AD WRNG immediately because 4 cm hail is well above the 2 cm severe-hail threshold.
Issue an AD WRNG for "approaching CB" because the cell's distance is decreasing.
Issue an AD WRNG with a 24 km distance threshold, the larger IMS courtesy radius.

name.text: L4-Q02 — Wind threshold: mean vs gust

questiontext.text: At LLBG the 10-minute mean surface wind is 17 kt, but the highest 3-second gust within the latest 10 minutes is 33 kt. Conditions are forecast to persist for the next 4 hours. Which is correct?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: The IMS wind criterion has two independent triggers joined by "and/or": 10-minute mean > 20 kt OR gusts > 30 kt. The gust (33 kt) is above its threshold, so AD WRNG issuance is required regardless of the mean. The 17 kt mean is below 20 kt and would not have triggered on its own. Waiting for the mean to also exceed 20 kt would mean withholding the warning during the very conditions it exists to flag.

answer.text: Issue an AD WRNG — the gust threshold (> 30 kt) is met regardless of the mean.
Do not issue — the 10-minute mean must exceed 20 kt for the wind criterion to be met.
Issue a WS WRNG instead, because gusts above 30 kt are wind shear by definition.
Issue only an AIRMET, because surface winds are an en-route phenomenon.

questiontext.text: A flight crew on departure from RWY26 at LLBG calls TWR at 0512Z to report moderate wind shear at 700 ft on climb-out. The forecaster confirms a synoptic situation that supports continued shear. Which is the correct basis indicator in the resulting WS WRNG, and what is the meaning?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: The WS WRNG vocabulary distinguishes FCST (forecaster's judgement), OBS (clear identification in MET data such as AMDAR, sonde, profiler), and REP AT (pilot report, followed by the time). The crew's call is a pilot report, so the warning should be issued with REP AT 0512Z. FCST would be appropriate if there was no pilot observation. OBS would be appropriate if the trigger were instrumented data (e.g., AMDAR), not a crew voice report. Combining FCST and OBS is not a defined option.

answer.text: REP AT 0512Z — the warning is based on a pilot report.
FCST — the forecaster's judgement that conditions support continued shear is what triggers the warning.
OBS — the pilot's call is a meteorological observation.
Combined FCST OBS — both forecaster judgement and an observation apply.

questiontext.text: An overnight sonde at LLBG shows a surface wind of 4 kt and a jet of 22 kt at 1100 ft AGL. The synoptic situation supports a stable nocturnal inversion. Which is the correct IMS action?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: The primary IMS WS WRNG LLJ trigger is peak ≥ 30 kt with axis below 2000 ft. 22 kt does not meet the primary trigger. However, the difference between surface (4 kt) and 500 m (≈ 1640 ft — close to the 1100 ft jet level) wind is 18 kt, which exceeds the 15 kt supporting indicator. With a matching synoptic, the IMS guidance says this can be treated as sufficient to issue a WS WRNG for the LLJ. Doing nothing under-warns; issuing an AIRMET miscategorises an aerodrome-scale phenomenon as en-route; issuing an AD WRNG for surface wind misses the shear nature of the hazard.

answer.text: Issue a WS WRNG — the > 15 kt surface-to-500 m wind difference with supporting synoptic is sufficient under IMS guidance.
Do not issue — the jet peak is below the 30 kt primary threshold.
Issue an AIRMET for MOD TURB — the LLJ is an en-route phenomenon.
Issue an AD WRNG for surface wind, even though the surface speed is only 4 kt.

questiontext.text: Convective cells over the central highlands are producing OCNL TS across that sub-area of the FIR, and one cell is forecast to track to within 12 km of the LLBG runway centre over the next 90 minutes. Which products should the IMS issue?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: Two distinct hazards are in play. OCNL TS across the sub-area is an AIRMET phenomenon (50–75% coverage falls into OCNL, which is below the SIGMET FRQ threshold). The cell tracking to within 12 km of the runway centre meets the IMS AD WRNG threshold (< 16 km). Both products are required: AD WRNG so the AFO communicates to airfield ops, AIRMET so en-route GA crossing the area receives the warning via VOLMET/AFTN. Issuing only the AD WRNG would leave foreign and en-route consumers blind; issuing only the AIRMET would leave the airfield without local-distribution coverage.

answer.text: AD WRNG (TS, < 16 km from LLBG) plus AIRMET (OCNL TS for the sub-area).
AD WRNG only — the cell is the airfield's problem.
AIRMET only — the AD WRNG threshold is not yet met until the cell crosses the runway.
AD WRNG plus SIGMET (FRQ TS) — any cell within 12 km of an aerodrome promotes the OCNL coverage to FRQ.

questiontext.text: An international dispatcher in Frankfurt is planning a flight to LLBG. Which IMS warning products will be available to her in the standard AFTN / VOLMET stream, and which will not?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: SIGMET and AIRMET are distributed internationally over AFTN and broadcast in VOLMET / D-VOLMET. AD WRNG and WS WRNG distribution is local only — they reach airfield operations, tower, and local ATS, but not foreign flight planning offices. This is exactly why coordination matters: an aerodrome hazard that also affects the en-route phase must be reflected in a SIGMET or AIRMET, otherwise the international consumer never learns of it.

answer.text: SIGMET and AIRMET reach Frankfurt via AFTN/VOLMET; AD WRNG and WS WRNG are local-distribution only.
All four products are distributed internationally over AFTN.
Only AD WRNG and WS WRNG reach Frankfurt — they are the aerodrome-specific products that flight planning needs.
None of the products are available outside Israel; foreign dispatchers rely on the TAF only.

name.text: L4-Q07 — When NOT to pair WS WRNG with an AIRMET

questiontext.text: The IMS issues a WS WRNG for LLBG because of a low-level jet (32 kt at 900 ft AGL, 5 kt at the surface). The FIR is otherwise quiet. Which is the correct accompanying action?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: The IMS coordination rule explicitly says that when a WS WRNG is issued for an aerodrome because of a low-level jet, no AIRMET or SIGMET is required. The LLJ is an aerodrome-scale phenomenon — it shears the approach and climb-out paths but does not, by itself, constitute a FIR-wide en-route hazard. Issuing an AIRMET would over-warn; issuing an AD WRNG would describe a different (surface-wind) hazard that does not apply here.

answer.text: No AIRMET or SIGMET is required — the LLJ is an aerodrome-scale phenomenon and the WS WRNG alone suffices.
Also issue an AIRMET for SFC WSPD ≥30KT because the jet is 32 kt.
Also issue an AD WRNG for surface wind, since a strong jet implies strong surface wind.
Also issue a SIGMET for SEV TURB, on the assumption that any LLJ produces severe turbulence.
